qc_i_g_mini_jumel_e.blurb: A south-facing sector of Mont-Césaire at Val-David in the Laurentians, holding about fifteen routes, mostly bolted sport lines with a handful of trad climbs. Grades run from easy 5.5-5.6 terrain up to 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.10 range, so it suits both newer leaders and those looking for something harder. Many lines begin on slabby ground that rewards good footwork. Because the wall faces south it heats up in summer, while whoever is belaying can stand in shade below. A stick clip is handy on the lower bolts. Expect a roughly quarter-hour uphill hike from the park's welcome area.

qc_19_le_fou.blurb: Le Fou is a numbered sector at Montagne d'Argent in the Laurentians, set a little away from the busier walls. It holds about fifteen routes split fairly evenly between sport and trad, including some two- and three-pitch lines and a top-rope option. Grades start with one very easy line, then cluster around 5.8 to 5.11. The climbing leans steep and crimpy, and the first pitch of many lines ends on a ledge, which makes it simple to set a top-rope. The surrounding mountain is mostly single-pitch with bolted anchors, a good fit for people newer to climbing.

qc_main_cliff_2.blurb: The main wall at the Belle Neige ski hill in the Laurentians, lying off to the left of the lodge. About fifteen routes, mostly bolted sport with a few trad lines. The spread is wide: a couple of 5.8-5.9 climbs for warming up, a solid block in the 5.10s and 5.11s, and several climbs at 5.12 and 5.13 for strong climbers. The wall stays in shade all day, which helps on hot afternoons but means it can feel cool early or late in the year. It makes a convenient stop for a short session near Val-Morin.

qc_d_le_grand_mur.blurb: The principal wall of the Pic aux Corbeaux cliffs at Mont Orford in the Eastern Townships, on gneiss. Fifteen routes, nearly all sport with a single trad line, and nothing easy: grades sit between 5.10 and 5.13, with most between 5.11 and 5.12. Face climbing dominates, and several lines can be done as two pitches or linked into one. The wall sits just beside the trailhead, but the hike up from the parking area is steep. Expect a destination for experienced sport climbers rather than beginners.

qc_bloc_du_v_lo.blurb: A boulder cluster on Mont-King at Val-David in the Laurentians, the largest group of problems in the Mont-King bouldering zone. It has about fifteen problems, a mix of traverses, dynos, a corner, a crack and sit-start variations. The range is broad: a few easy problems near V0, several mid-grade ones, and a sizable group from V6 to V8, so strong boulderers will find plenty. It also works as a warm-up spot before heading deeper into Mont-King. From the signed trail, the boulders are a short two-minute uphill walk after the fork for the neighbouring sector.
